name: Columbia
story:
Gold was found at Columbia on March 27, 1850. The gold lay in the surface gravels, but there was little water to wash them with, so miners built a network of aqueducts to bring it in, at a cost of more than a million dollars. Between 1850 and the early 1900s at least $87 million in gold came out of the surrounding hills.
The bedrock here is limestone, and limestone dissolves into knobs, pinnacles and deep potholes. The potholes held enormously rich gravel. Miners dug it out of the crevices and then washed the rest away with water cannons, and the pinnacles were left standing: the "rock gardens" that visitors walk among today.
In the lidar they are the rough, dark ground running south and east of the old town. The water-filled pit east of them is an old quarry in the same limestone; marble has long been quarried around Columbia. The long flat strip on the west side is Columbia Airport's runway.

sources.name: Columbia State Historic Park brochure (California State Parks)

name: Harvard Pit, Jamestown Mine
story:
The Harvard is the modern end of Mother Lode mining. Underground mines followed the gold here in the old days; from 1986 to 1994 Sonora Mining Corporation dug out the gold-bearing rock along the Melones fault from the top instead, in an open pit about 830 m long, 460 m wide and 185 m deep.
When mining ended, the pit began to fill. By November 2000 the lake was about 90 m (300 ft) deep. In 1998 and 1999 the USGS measured 720 to 1,100 parts per billion of arsenic in its water. Eleven evaporators now sit in the pit to keep the level down.
In the lidar the lake is a hole: laser light doesn't come back from water. North of it the waste rock stands in stepped dumps cut by haul roads, and the big flat oval to the west is the tailings facility. Its pond leaked, so it was drained, graded, capped with clay, covered with topsoil and seeded.
